entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8042"/><div sID="gen12490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8042"/>2. A profane sentiment if severed from its connection; but just in its bearing on Solomon's scope. If religion were not taken into account (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ec 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">19</reference>), to die as soon as possible would be desirable, so as not to suffer or witness "oppressions"; and still more so, not to be born at all (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ec 7:1</reference>). Job (<reference osisRef="Job.3.12">Job 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">21:7</reference>), David (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.3">Psa 73:3</reference>, &c.), Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jr 12:1</reference>), Habakkuk (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Ha 1:13</reference>), all passed through the same perplexity, until they went into the sanctuary, and looked beyond the present to the "judgment" (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Psa 73:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">Ha 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">18</reference>). Then they saw the need of delay, before completely punishing the wicked, to give space for repentance, or else for accumulation of wrath (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.15">Ro 2:15</reference>); and before completely rewarding the godly, to give room for faith and perseverance in tribulation (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.7-Ps.92.12">Psa 92:7-12</reference>). Earnests, however, are often even now given, by partial judgments of the future, to assure us, in spite of difficulties, that God governs the earth. <div eID="gen12490" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8053"/><div sID="gen12507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8053"/>13. The "threefold cord" [Ec 4:12] of social ties suggests the subject of civil government. In this case too, he concludes that kingly power confers no lasting happiness. The "wise" child, though a supposed case of Solomon, answers, in the event foreseen by the Holy Ghost, to Jeroboam, then a poor but valiant youth, once a "servant" of Solomon, and (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.26-1Kgs.11.40">1Ki 11:26-40</reference>) appointed by God through the prophet Ahijah to be heir of the kingdom of the ten tribes about to be rent from Rehoboam. The "old and foolish king" answers to Solomon himself, who had lost his wisdom, when, in defiance of two warnings of God (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.14">1Ki 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.2-1Kgs.9.9">9:2-9</reference>), he forsook God.<div eID="gen12507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will no more be admonished--</hi>knows not yet how to take warning (see Margin) God had by Ahijah already intimated the judgment coming on Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.11-1Kgs.11.13">1Ki 11:11-13</reference>). <div eID="gen12508" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 13. The "threefold cord" [Ec 4:12] of social ties suggests the subject of civil government. In this case too, he concludes that kingly power confers no lasting happiness. The "wise" child, though a supposed case of Solomon, answers, in the event foreseen by the Holy Ghost, to Jeroboam, then a poor but valiant youth, once a "servant" of Solomon, and ( 1Ki 11:26-40 ) appointed by God through the prophet Ahijah to be heir of the kingdom of the ten tribes about to be rent from Rehoboam. The "old and foolish king" answers to Solomon himself, who had lost his wisdom, when, in defiance of two warnings of God ( 1Ki 3:14 ; 9:2-9 ), he forsook God. will no more be admonished-- knows not yet how to take warning (see Margin) God had by Ahijah already intimated the judgment coming on Solomon ( 1Ki 11:11-13 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8054"/><div sID="gen12509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8054"/><hi type="bold">14. out of prison--</hi>Solomon uses this phrase of a supposed case; for example, Joseph raised from a dungeon to be lord of Egypt. His words are at the same time so framed by the Holy Ghost that they answer virtually to Jeroboam, who fled to escape a "prison" and death from Solomon, to Shishak of Egypt (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.40">1Ki 11:40</reference>). This unconscious presaging of his own doom, and that of Rehoboam, constitutes the irony. David's elevation from poverty and exile, under Saul (which may have been before Solomon's mind), had so far their counterpart in that of Jeroboam.<div eID="gen12509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whereas ... becometh poor--</hi>rather, "though he (the youth) was born poor in his kingdom" (in the land where afterwards he was to reign). <div eID="gen12510" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 14. out of prison-- Solomon uses this phrase of a supposed case; for example, Joseph raised from a dungeon to be lord of Egypt. His words are at the same time so framed by the Holy Ghost that they answer virtually to Jeroboam, who fled to escape a "prison" and death from Solomon, to Shishak of Egypt ( 1Ki 11:40 ). This unconscious presaging of his own doom, and that of Rehoboam, constitutes the irony. David's elevation from poverty and exile, under Saul (which may have been before Solomon's mind), had so far their counterpart in that of Jeroboam. whereas ... becometh poor-- rather, "though he (the youth) was born poor in his kingdom" (in the land where afterwards he was to reign).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8056"/><div sID="gen12513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8056"/>16. Notwithstanding their now worshipping the rising sun, the heir-apparent, I reflected that "there were no bounds, no stability (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.6">2Sa 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1">20:1</reference>), no check on the love of innovation, of all that have been before them," that is, the past generation; so<div eID="gen12513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also they that come after--</hi>that is, the next generation,<div eID="gen12514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall not rejoice in him--</hi>namely, Rehoboam. The parallel, "shall not rejoice," fixes the sense of "no bounds," no permanent adherence, though now men rejoice in him. <chapter eID="Eccl.4"/>
entries.content_plain: 16. Notwithstanding their now worshipping the rising sun, the heir-apparent, I reflected that "there were no bounds, no stability ( 2Sa 15:6 ; 20:1 ), no check on the love of innovation, of all that have been before them," that is, the past generation; so also they that come after-- that is, the next generation, shall not rejoice in him-- namely, Rehoboam. The parallel, "shall not rejoice," fixes the sense of "no bounds," no permanent adherence, though now men rejoice in him.
